summary: Describes the Access Node Control Protocol, which runs between a Network Access Server and an access node such as a DSLAM in a broadband network. It supports operations related to quality of service, services, and subscribers, and includes capabilities beyond the base protocol.

eli5.summary: Broadband equipment close to your home needs instructions from a central machine. ANCP is the language they use, like a manager radioing a worker at a street cabinet to adjust things.

questions: how does a nas control a dslam
what is the ancp adjacency protocol
how does a nas configure a dslam line
subtitle: The control protocol that lets a broadband gateway and the DSLAM at the street cabinet talk to each other about lines, rates and tests.

tldr.problem: A Network Access Server that handles quality of service for subscribers cannot see what the Access Node, such as a DSLAM, is doing with each DSL line, and cannot easily change it.
tldr.mechanism: ANCP opens a TCP session from the Access Node to the NAS, negotiates capabilities with an adjacency handshake, and then exchanges TLV-based messages for topology discovery, line configuration and remote line testing.
tldr.outcome: It gives operators a standard way to pass line rates and state upward and service profiles and test requests downward. It is based on GSMPv3 but is not interoperable with it, and RFC 7256 updates this RFC.

today: RFC 6320 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7256. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What ANCP Is and Where It Came From
sections.content:
The Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) is a control plane between a service-oriented layer 3 edge device, the Network Access Server (NAS), and a layer 2 Access Node (AN), for example a Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer (DSLAM). It is used for operations related to quality of service, services and subscriptions. The requirements and context are in RFC 5851.

ANCP serves control applications on each side. Each side has an ANCP agent, a logical entity that implements the protocol. The RFC specifies the agents and their messages, not the control applications themselves, though it gives informative descriptions to explain context.

The protocol began as implementations based on General Switch Management Protocol version 3 (GSMPv3, RFC 3292). So many extensions and changes were added that the two are not interoperable, yet ANCP kept GSMP's TCP port and encapsulation. To tell them apart, a joint GSMP/ANCP version registry was created: GSMP uses versions 1 through 3 and ANCP starts at version 50. The unused fields in ANCP headers are a trace of this heritage.
sections.eli5: ANCP is a language for two machines in a phone network to chat. It grew out of an older language, but changed so much that the two cannot understand each other, so it got its own version number.

sections.title: The Broadband Access Network
sections.content:
The Access Node terminates the DSL signal and is the first point where traffic from many DSL lines is aggregated onto a single network. The NAS aggregates subscriber traffic from many Access Nodes and is also the enforcement point for policy management and IP quality of service. A Home Gateway sits at the customer end, and the RFC calls the whole path from NAS to AN the access aggregation network.

The RFC describes two kinds of aggregation. In an ATM-based network the NAS uses hierarchical scheduling so that downstream traffic does not queue up too deeply farther down the ATM network. In an Ethernet-based network, VLAN tagging is used. Stacked tags can act like virtual paths and circuits: the outer VLAN between a DSLAM and a NAS, and the inner VLAN per DSL line (the 1:1 model). Alternatively, many subscribers behind a DSLAM can share one VLAN (the N:1 model).

These models matter because ANCP must be able to identify a particular access line in whichever of them is in use.
sections.eli5: Think of a street cabinet where lots of home phone lines meet, and a bigger exchange that manages the traffic from many cabinets. ANCP lets the exchange and the cabinet coordinate.

sections.title: Transport and the Adjacency Handshake
sections.content:
ANCP messages travel over TCP, with IPsec and IKEv2 required for security. Each ANCP message is prefixed with a 4-byte header: an Identifier that MUST be 0x880C and a Length giving the size of the ANCP message in bytes. The Access Node MUST initiate the TCP session to the NAS using destination port 6068, and the NAS MUST listen on that port. This avoids having to provision every AN's address on the NAS. Text fields use UTF-8, and a receiver must not assume they are zero-terminated. Reserved and unused fields are set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

Once TCP is up, both sides run the adjacency protocol before sending anything else. Each peer sends a SYN, gets a SYNACK and completes with an ACK. The exchange teaches each side the other's name, port and instance, and negotiates the version, timer, partition and the set of capabilities. A mismatch triggers an RSTACK, which restarts the process. The three states are SYNSENT, SYNRCVD and ESTAB.

The Timer field is in units of 100 ms with a default of 250, which is 25 seconds. After synchronization, an ACK exchange acts as a liveness test. Loss of synchronization MAY be declared if no valid ANCP message arrives for more than three times the timer, or if a state mismatch is found. If the set of agreed capabilities is empty, the sender raises an alarm and halts the adjacency procedure.

Each capability has a type. The RFC defines three, all for DSL access: DSL Topology Discovery (0x01), DSL Line Configuration (0x02) and DSL Remote Line Connectivity Testing (0x04). If several NASs are attached to one AN partition, the AN sends an Adjacency Update message (type 85) so each knows how many adjacencies exist.
sections.eli5: Before they talk, the two machines shake hands: hello, hello back, nice to meet you. They agree on what jobs they both know how to do, and then keep checking now and then that the other is still there.

sections.title: Message Header, TLVs and Generic Messages
sections.content:
After adjacency, all ANCP messages share one general header: Version (the negotiated one), Message Type, a 4-bit Result, a 12-bit Result Code, Partition ID, a 24-bit Transaction Identifier, an I flag with a 15-bit sub-message number, and a Length. The I flag and sub-message number come from GSMPv3 fragmentation; ANCP sets both to 1 because TCP makes fragmentation unnecessary.

The Result field says what kind of reply a request wants (Ignore 0x0, Nack 0x1, AckAll 0x2) and, in a response, whether it worked (Success 0x3, Failure 0x4). The Transaction Identifier lets a sender match a response to its request; request IDs normally count up from 1 and responses copy the value, while event messages use zero.

After the fixed fields comes the payload: zero or more fixed fields followed by Type-Length-Value (TLV) structures. A TLV has a 16-bit type, a 16-bit length and a value padded with zeroes to a 4-byte boundary. A TLV may contain other TLVs, and a receiver that does not understand a TLV MUST silently ignore it.

Two general messages are defined. The Provisioning message (type 93) is sent by the NAS to push global information to the AN. The Generic Response message (type 91) reports success or failure, always carries a Status-Info TLV on failure, and MUST NOT trigger an error response to itself, which prevents error loops. The general-purpose TLVs are Target (0x1000), Command (0x0011) and Status-Info (0x0106), which holds a human-readable message that starts with a language tag.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with the same label saying what kind it is and how it went. After the label come little labelled boxes of information, and a receiver just skips any box it does not recognise.

sections.title: Result Codes
sections.content:
The Result Code field gives more detail in a response. The RFC defines the codes together with where the problem is detected, what extra information the reply must carry, and what the receiving agent is recommended to do. Examples include 0x2 (invalid request message, usually a race condition, which may be resent once after a short delay), 0x13 (out of resources, reported only by the AN) and 0x53 (malformed message, which SHOULD be re-sent once to rule out corruption in transit).

Two codes deal with missing or bad TLVs. For 0x54 (mandatory TLV missing) the response MUST contain a Status-Info TLV with an empty instance of each missing TLV. For 0x55 (invalid TLV contents) it MUST contain the erroneous TLVs copied from the request. Code 0x500 means one or more of the specified ports do not exist, and 0x6 means one or more ports are down.

For failures that persist, the agent may reset the adjacency with an RSTACK, and if that does not help it SHOULD raise an alarm to management and stop operating. A count of how often each non-zero code was received SHOULD be made available for management.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the reply includes a number saying what, like a doctor's note, and the receiver knows whether to try again once or to tell a person.

sections.title: The Three DSL Capabilities
sections.content:
First, every message about a line must say which line. Four TLVs do that: Access-Loop-Circuit-ID (user side, up to 63 bytes of ASCII), Access-Aggregation-Circuit-ID-ASCII and its binary twin (NAS side, carrying VLAN identifiers or ATM VPI and VCI), and Access-Loop-Remote-ID (an operator string for the user). To the protocol they are opaque; they match the identifiers used in DHCP Option 82.

Topology discovery. The AN sends a Port Up (type 80) or Port Down (type 81) event message when a line synchronizes, resynchronizes or drops, and for each line when an adjacency starts. Port Up MUST carry a DSL-Line-Attributes TLV (0x0004), which wraps attributes such as actual, minimum, maximum and attainable data rates upstream and downstream in kbits/s, interleaving delays in ms, line state (SHOWTIME, IDLE or SILENT) and DSL type (such as ADSL2+ or VDSL2). The NAS uses these to adjust its queuing and scheduling for that line. The AN SHOULD dampen the rate of such reports.

Line configuration. The NAS sends a Port Management message (type 32) with Function set to 8 (Configure Connection Service Data). The one TLV defined is Service-Profile-Name (0x0005, up to 64 bytes), a reference to a profile already configured on the DSLAM, learned from a policy server after the subscriber is authorized.

Remote line testing. The same Port Management message with Function 9 (Remote Loopback) asks the AN to run a loopback test. The NAS may send an OAM-Loopback-Test-Parameters TLV with a Count (SHOULD be above 0 and at most 32) and a Timeout in seconds, plus an 8-byte Opaque-Data TLV copied back in the reply. The AN replies later, when its control application has a result, and may include a UTF-8 response string of up to 128 bytes. Result codes 0x501 to 0x509 report outcomes such as timeout, line state and invalid test parameter.
sections.eli5: The street cabinet tells the exchange when a line wakes up or goes quiet and how fast it runs. The exchange can say which settings package to use for a customer, and can ask the cabinet to test a line.

sections.title: Security: IPsec and IKEv2
sections.content:
The RFC takes the security requirements from RFC 5713. The protocol MUST offer mutual authentication of AN and NAS, authorization, replay protection, data-origin authentication and robustness against denial of service, and SHOULD offer confidentiality.

Both TLS and IPsec could meet most of these, but TLS was rejected. The adjacency is a prime target: an attacker who can tear it down either forces the AN to clear its state or opens up mismatches between the AN's and NAS's views of state. That can be done by tampering with messages or by attacking the TCP session, and TLS protects message contents but not the TCP connection. Hence ANCP MUST run over IPsec with IKEv2.

In detail, IPsec runs in transport mode, because the AN and NAS are the path's endpoints. ESP MUST be used, configured for confidentiality, integrity and anti-replay. IKEv2 is required for mutual authentication and authorization, and the AN MUST be the initiator of the IKEv2 conversation. Because AN and NAS may be in different trust domains, certificates may be the most practical approach, but that is left to operators.
sections.eli5: The messages control real equipment, so they travel in a locked, tamper-proof pouch. Both sides must prove who they are first, and the pouch protects the whole delivery, not just the letter inside.
